<header class="dg-head dg-head-section"><p class="dg-kicker">Appendix B <span class="dg-sep">•</span> <a href="index.html">Proofs &amp; Comments</a></p><h1 class="dg-title"><span class="dg-secnum">B.12</span> Sylvester’s law of inertia (§<a class="dg-xref" href="../metric/metric.html#subsection_Metric_Signature" data-kind="subsection" data-label="subsection_Metric_Signature">7.1.1</a>)</h1></header>
<p>Let <span class="math inline">\((V, \oplus, \odot)\)</span> be an <span class="math inline">\(\mathbb{R}\)</span>-vector space of dimension <span class="math inline">\(d \geq 1\)</span> (we write <span class="math inline">\(+\)</span> and juxtaposition for its operations) and let <span class="math display">\begin{align*}
    b : V \times V             &amp;\xlongrightarrow{\substack{\sim \\ \sim}} \mathbb{R} \\
    (\mathcal{X}, \mathcal{Y}) &amp;\longmapsto b(\mathcal{X}, \mathcal{Y})
\end{align*}</span> be a symmetric bilinear form which is non-degenerate: <span class="math inline">\(b(\mathcal{X}, \mathcal{Y}) = 0\)</span> for all <span class="math inline">\(\mathcal{Y} \in V\)</span> implies <span class="math inline">\(\mathcal{X} = 0\)</span>. The case of interest in Chapter <a class="dg-xref" href="../metric/index.html" data-kind="chapter" data-label="chapter_Metric">7</a> is <span class="math inline">\(V = T_p\mathcal{M}\)</span> and <span class="math inline">\(b = g_p\)</span>.</p>
<div class="dg-skip dg-medskip"></div>
<p><strong>Statement.</strong></p>
<ol class="dg-enumerate dg-depth-1">
<li class="dg-labelled"><span class="dg-item-label">(i)</span> <p><em>Existence:</em> there exists a basis <span class="math inline">\(\{ \hat{e}_1, \dots, \hat{e}_d \}\)</span> of <span class="math inline">\(V\)</span> such that <span class="math inline">\(b(\hat{e}_a, \hat{e}_b) = 0\)</span> for <span class="math inline">\(a \neq b\)</span> and <span class="math inline">\(b(\hat{e}_a, \hat{e}_a) \in \{+1, -1\}\)</span>.</p></li>
<li class="dg-labelled"><span class="dg-item-label">(ii)</span> <p><em>Uniqueness of the signs:</em> the number <span class="math inline">\(n_+\)</span> of basis vectors with <span class="math inline">\(b(\hat{e}_a, \hat{e}_a) = +1\)</span>, and hence the number <span class="math inline">\(n_- = d - n_+\)</span> of those with <span class="math inline">\(b(\hat{e}_a, \hat{e}_a) = -1\)</span>, is the same for every basis as in (i).</p></li>
</ol>
<div class="dg-skip dg-medskip"></div>
<p><strong>Proof of (i)</strong>, by induction on <span class="math inline">\(d\)</span>.</p>
<ul class="dg-itemize dg-depth-1">
<li><p><em>There is a vector <span class="math inline">\(\mathcal{X}_0\)</span> with <span class="math inline">\(b(\mathcal{X}_0, \mathcal{X}_0) \neq 0\)</span>.</em> Otherwise, by bilinearity and symmetry (polarization),  <span class="math display">\[
            b(\mathcal{X}, \mathcal{Y})
            = \tfrac{1}{2} \Big[ b(\mathcal{X} + \mathcal{Y}, \mathcal{X} + \mathcal{Y}) - b(\mathcal{X}, \mathcal{X}) - b(\mathcal{Y}, \mathcal{Y}) \Big]
            = 0 \qquad \forall \, \mathcal{X}, \mathcal{Y} \in V,
        \]</span>  contradicting non-degeneracy, since <span class="math inline">\(V \neq \{0\}\)</span>.</p></li>
<li><p><em>Normalization.</em> Set <span class="math inline">\(\hat{e}_1 \coloneqq \mathcal{X}_0 / \sqrt{|b(\mathcal{X}_0, \mathcal{X}_0)|}\)</span>. Then <span class="math inline">\(b(\hat{e}_1, \hat{e}_1) = b(\mathcal{X}_0, \mathcal{X}_0) / |b(\mathcal{X}_0, \mathcal{X}_0)| = \pm 1\)</span>. If <span class="math inline">\(d = 1\)</span>, we are done.</p></li>
<li><p><em>Splitting off <span class="math inline">\(\hat{e}_1\)</span>.</em> Let <span class="math inline">\(W \coloneqq \{ \mathcal{W} \in V \mid b(\hat{e}_1, \mathcal{W}) = 0 \}\)</span>, the kernel of the linear map <span class="math inline">\(b(\hat{e}_1, \cdot) : V \to \mathbb{R}\)</span>. This map is non-zero (it takes the value <span class="math inline">\(\pm 1\)</span> on <span class="math inline">\(\hat{e}_1\)</span>), hence surjective, and <span class="math inline">\(\dim W = d - 1\)</span> by rank–nullity. Every <span class="math inline">\(\mathcal{X} \in V\)</span> decomposes uniquely as  <span class="math display">\[
            \mathcal{X} = \alpha \, \hat{e}_1 + \mathcal{W},
            \qquad
            \alpha \coloneqq \frac{b(\hat{e}_1, \mathcal{X})}{b(\hat{e}_1, \hat{e}_1)},
            \qquad
            \mathcal{W} \coloneqq \mathcal{X} - \alpha \, \hat{e}_1 \in W,
        \]</span>  where <span class="math inline">\(b(\hat{e}_1, \mathcal{W}) = b(\hat{e}_1, \mathcal{X}) - \alpha \, b(\hat{e}_1, \hat{e}_1) = 0\)</span>, and uniqueness follows by applying <span class="math inline">\(b(\hat{e}_1, \cdot)\)</span> to two such decompositions.</p></li>
<li><p><em><span class="math inline">\(b\)</span> restricted to <span class="math inline">\(W\)</span> is non-degenerate.</em> If <span class="math inline">\(\mathcal{W}_0 \in W\)</span> satisfies <span class="math inline">\(b(\mathcal{W}_0, \mathcal{W}) = 0\)</span> for all <span class="math inline">\(\mathcal{W} \in W\)</span>, then for every <span class="math inline">\(\mathcal{X} = \alpha \, \hat{e}_1 + \mathcal{W}\)</span>,  <span class="math display">\[
            b(\mathcal{W}_0, \mathcal{X}) = \alpha \, \underbrace{b(\mathcal{W}_0, \hat{e}_1)}_{= \, b(\hat{e}_1, \mathcal{W}_0) \, = \, 0} + \, b(\mathcal{W}_0, \mathcal{W}) = 0,
        \]</span>  so <span class="math inline">\(\mathcal{W}_0 = 0\)</span> by non-degeneracy of <span class="math inline">\(b\)</span> on <span class="math inline">\(V\)</span>.</p></li>
<li><p><em>Induction.</em> Applying the induction hypothesis to <span class="math inline">\((W, b|_{W \times W})\)</span> yields a basis <span class="math inline">\(\{ \hat{e}_2, \dots, \hat{e}_d \}\)</span> of <span class="math inline">\(W\)</span> with the required properties. Its elements satisfy <span class="math inline">\(b(\hat{e}_1, \hat{e}_a) = 0\)</span> because they lie in <span class="math inline">\(W\)</span>, and by the unique decomposition above, <span class="math inline">\(\{ \hat{e}_1, \dots, \hat{e}_d \}\)</span> is a basis of <span class="math inline">\(V\)</span>. <span class="math inline">\(\square\)</span></p></li>
</ul>
<div class="dg-skip dg-medskip"></div>
<p><strong>Proof of (ii).</strong> Let <span class="math inline">\(\{ \hat{e}_a \}\)</span> and <span class="math inline">\(\{ \hat{e}'_a \}\)</span> be two bases as in (i), with <span class="math inline">\(n_+\)</span> and <span class="math inline">\(n'_+\)</span> positive entries, respectively. Consider the subspaces <span class="math display">\[
    V_+ \coloneqq \operatorname{span}\{ \hat{e}_a \mid b(\hat{e}_a, \hat{e}_a) = +1 \},
    \qquad
    V'_- \coloneqq \operatorname{span}\{ \hat{e}'_a \mid b(\hat{e}'_a, \hat{e}'_a) = -1 \},
\]</span> of dimensions <span class="math inline">\(n_+\)</span> and <span class="math inline">\(d - n'_+\)</span>. For a non-zero <span class="math inline">\(\mathcal{X} = \sum_a \alpha^a \, \hat{e}_a \in V_+\)</span> (sum over the positive basis vectors only), <span class="math inline">\(b(\mathcal{X}, \mathcal{X}) = \sum_a (\alpha^a)^2 &gt; 0\)</span>, while for a non-zero <span class="math inline">\(\mathcal{Y} = \sum_a \beta^a \, \hat{e}'_a \in V'_-\)</span>, <span class="math inline">\(b(\mathcal{Y}, \mathcal{Y}) = -\sum_a (\beta^a)^2 &lt; 0\)</span>. Hence <span class="math inline">\(V_+ \cap V'_- = \{0\}\)</span>, and the dimension of the subspace <span class="math inline">\(V_+ + V'_- \subseteq V\)</span> is <span class="math display">\[
    \dim(V_+ + V'_-) = \dim V_+ + \dim V'_- - \dim(V_+ \cap V'_-) = n_+ + (d - n'_+) \leq d
    \quad \longrightarrow \quad n_+ \leq n'_+ .
\]</span> Exchanging the roles of the two bases gives <span class="math inline">\(n'_+ \leq n_+\)</span>, so <span class="math inline">\(n_+ = n'_+\)</span>. <span class="math inline">\(\square\)</span></p>
<div class="dg-skip dg-medskip"></div>
<p><strong>Remark (eigenvalues).</strong> Given any basis of <span class="math inline">\(V\)</span>, the matrix <span class="math inline">\(\mathbf{B}\)</span> of entries <span class="math inline">\(b(\hat{x}_i, \hat{x}_j)\)</span> is real and symmetric, so it can be diagonalized by an orthogonal matrix <span class="math inline">\(\mathbf{O}\)</span>, <span class="math inline">\(\mathbf{O}^{\mathsf{T}} \mathbf{B} \, \mathbf{O} = \operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_d)\)</span>. Since <span class="math inline">\(\mathbf{O}^{\mathsf{T}} = \mathbf{O}^{-1}\)</span>, this is at the same time a change of basis for <span class="math inline">\(b\)</span> (a congruence), and rescaling the new basis vectors by <span class="math inline">\(1/\sqrt{|\lambda_a|}\)</span> produces a basis as in (i). By (ii), <span class="math inline">\(n_+\)</span> is therefore the number of positive eigenvalues of <span class="math inline">\(\mathbf{B}\)</span>, whichever basis was used to write it down. The eigenvalues themselves, however, do depend on the basis.</p>
<div class="dg-skip dg-medskip"></div>
<p><strong>Remark (realization by a chart).</strong> In the case <span class="math inline">\(V = T_p\mathcal{M}\)</span>, <span class="math inline">\(b = g_p\)</span>, the basis of (i) can always be realized as the chart-induced basis at <span class="math inline">\(p\)</span> of a suitable chart. Given any chart <span class="math inline">\((\mathcal{U}, \mathscr{X})\)</span> around <span class="math inline">\(p\)</span>, write <span class="math inline">\(\hat{e}_a = A^i{}_a \, (\partial x_i)_p\)</span>, with <span class="math inline">\((A^i{}_a)\)</span> an invertible matrix. The chart <span class="math display">\[
    \mathscr{Y}^a \coloneqq (A^{-1})^a{}_i \, \big( \mathscr{X}^i - \mathscr{X}^i(p) \big),
\]</span> obtained from <span class="math inline">\(\mathscr{X}\)</span> by a linear (hence <span class="math inline">\(C^\infty\)</span>-compatible) change of chart, satisfies <span class="math display">\[
    (\partial y_a)_p = A^i{}_a \, (\partial x_i)_p = \hat{e}_a ,
\]</span> since <span class="math inline">\((\partial x_i)_p = \big( \partial \mathscr{Y}^a / \partial \mathscr{X}^i \big)_p \, (\partial y_a)_p = (A^{-1})^a{}_i \, (\partial y_a)_p\)</span>. In this chart, the components of the metric at <span class="math inline">\(p\)</span> are diagonal, <span class="math inline">\(g_{ab}(p) = 0\)</span> for <span class="math inline">\(a \neq b\)</span>, with <span class="math inline">\(g_{aa}(p) = \pm 1\)</span>.</p>
